summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both sources audited for this province are national in scope, and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, protection scheme or service, so the assessment rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed on 6 December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview gives up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage, every sexual act by a same-sex couple falls within the outside-marriage offence. Reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Criminalisation below the national level exists in two provinces. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, on top of the national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in February 2025 two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there. The Sharia-based outlier is Aceh, not Maluku, and no equivalent Maluku ordinance appears in the sources.

Physical risk is rising. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions, and that the surge follows officials' public condemnations together with a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party', arresting 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and screening follow narrow rules. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians, operating in nine provinces. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The country's posture on LGBT rights is restrictive across institutions. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected, by five votes to four, a petition to criminalise homosexuality, leaving the outside-marriage offence and provincial religious law as the operative routes to prosecution. Indonesia also voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public opinion aligns with the legal direction: a 2023 Pew Research survey found that 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage. Reporting in August 2026 ties the increase in mob attacks on transgender people directly to official rhetoric and to the October 2025 presidential decree that places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy.

The provincial layer differs sharply by location. Aceh and South Sumatra carry their own same-sex offences and Aceh imposes corporal punishment, while provinces such as Maluku rely on the national penal code and the morality statutes alone. Visitors moving between provinces therefore face different penalties for the same conduct.

Raids have targeted gatherings that break no specific law, as Amnesty International argued over the 22 June 2025 villa operation, and the enforcement pattern is selective rather than systematic according to the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Maluku live under the national penal code provision on sex outside marriage, which applies to unmarried couples and, because same-sex marriage is unavailable, to every same-sex couple. The sources give two penalty figures for the offence: up to two years' imprisonment in the Human Dignity Trust profile, and up to one year where an immediate family member is the complainant.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex reassignment surgery and with a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female'. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians, a route documented in nine provinces.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both. Transgender Indonesians therefore rely on individual complaints and on civil-society advocacy rather than on a statutory protection scheme.

Expression offences reach residents directly: the 2006 pornography law covers written and audio-visual material suggesting same-sex relations, and broadcast regulators have restricted LGBTQ content since March 2016. Websites and apps have also been blocked, including Grindr.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Maluku-specific finding is available. Neither audited source records a provincial ordinance, a police raid, a caning, a protection scheme or a trans service operating in Maluku, and the sources cited for this province are national in scope. Whether the nine provinces covered by the Ministry of Home Affairs ID-card outreach include Maluku is not stated.

The sources differ on the penalty for sex outside marriage, giving two years in one profile and one year where an immediate family member complains in another; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

Entry and border screening for trans visitors, treatment of passports with changed markers, availability of trans-specific healthcare in Maluku, and any provincial-level police practice are not sourced here. The status of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour is recorded only as under discussion, with no outcome available.
